lockmem-rs: Lock virtual memory regions of an arbitrary process into its working set.

This utility allows you to lock every available memory regions of an arbitrary process into its working set. It uses ntdll!NtLockVirtualMemory (the system call used internally by VirtualLock) to lock memory ranges and GetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx / SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx to increase the size of the process working set.

The Windows kernel guarantees that those pages will stay resident in memory, not written to the pagefile and not incur a page fault on access.

items.content:
RT @marcosd4h: Been digging deep into the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP) in Win11 25H2, definitely one of the most fascinating security features Microsoft has built in a while.

The concept is neat: compile rules to decision graphs in user mode, hand them to wesp.sys, and let the kernel evaluate them in-path while telemetry streams asynchronously in the background.

I did an AI-assisted reverse engineering dive into the whole stack (wesp.sys, espclient.dll, and wesp_elam.sys), documented the wire protocols, disposition tables, and the enforcement gate, and built esptool, a research harness with 118 XML rule docs so anyone can test live telemetry and in-kernel blocking.

Repo: https://t.co/ZPYPHfmCP4

Tech doc:  https://t.co/P2s4geHEsI

Thanks to @yarden_shafir for putting this on my radar

items.content:
Then we have benchmarks.

Geekbench -> Measures CPU performance across a collection of compute workloads and reports single-core and multi-core scores.

Cinebench -> Uses workloads based on Maxon's Cinema 4D rendering technology. It is commonly used for comparing CPU rendering performance, while newer versions also support GPU testing.

3DMark -> A collection of benchmarks mainly used to measure GPU, graphics and gaming-related performance.

Speedometer -> Measures browser and web application responsiveness using simulated user interactions.

SPEC CPU -> A standardized benchmark suite widely used for evaluating CPU-intensive compute performance.

MLPerf -> A family of standardized machine-learning benchmarks covering areas such as AI training and inference.

Then there are performance numbers you will constantly see:

IPC -> Instructions Per Cycle

GHz -> Clock frequency

TDP -> A thermal/power design metric. The exact definition can vary between vendors.

TOPS -> Trillions of operations per second. Commonly used when talking about AI accelerators, but the operation type and precision matter.

TFLOPS -> Trillions of floating-point operations per second.

Memory bandwidth -> How much data can be transferred to/from memory per second.

Cache -> Small, fast memory close to processor cores that reduces the need to repeatedly access slower main memory.

Performance/Watt -> How much useful performance a system delivers for the power it consumes.

And another important distinction:

Arm and x86 are instruction set architecture families.

The ISA defines the software-visible instruction set and architectural behavior.

Microarchitecture is how a particular processor actually implements that ISA internally.

Pipeline design, execution units, caches, branch predictors, instruction scheduling and many other things live at this level.

Then there is the manufacturing process.

Then packaging.

Then memory.

Then firmware and software.

And finally the device you actually use.

Architecture + process technology + memory + packaging + power + cooling + software + workload all come together to determine the performance you actually see.

Once you start separating these layers, semiconductor news becomes much easier to understand.
items.author: OSdev_

items.content:
You read that a new chip uses N2P, has 50 TOPS of AI performance, uses HBM, beats another CPU in Geekbench and is built for hyperscalers.

But what do any of these words actually mean?

If you are new to the semiconductor industry, chip news can feel like it expects you to already know another language.

ASIC, SoC, NPU, hyperscaler, N2P, 18A, HBM, chiplets, Geekbench, Cinebench, Speedometer...

So here is a simple guide to the terms you will see again and again:

ASIC -> Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip designed for a specific application or set of functions instead of general-purpose computing.

Many dedicated AI accelerators are ASICs.

FPGA -> Field-Programmable Gate Array. A chip whose programmable logic and interconnect can be configured after manufacturing. This makes it useful for prototyping and workloads where hardware flexibility matters.

SoC -> System on Chip. An integrated circuit that combines major parts of a computing system, such as CPU cores, GPU, NPU, memory controllers, media engines, security blocks and I/O.

AI accelerator -> A broad term for hardware optimized for AI computation. GPUs, NPUs and dedicated ASICs can all be AI accelerators.

Hyperscaler -> A company operating computing infrastructure at enormous scale, usually across huge fleets of servers and data centers.

Companies at this scale may even design their own processors or AI accelerators because optimizing hardware for their workloads can improve performance, power efficiency and cost.

Then you will constantly see names like:

TSMC N3P
TSMC N2 / N2P
Intel 18A
Intel 14A

These are semiconductor manufacturing process technology names.

One important thing:

3nm, 2nm or 18A should NOT be interpreted as the literal size of a transistor.

Modern node names represent generations of manufacturing technology rather than one specific physical dimension.

A newer process can improve transistor density, performance and/or power efficiency. But a newer process does NOT automatically mean the final chip will be faster. The architecture still matters.

You will also hear:

FinFET -> A transistor structure where the gate controls multiple sides of a fin-shaped channel.

GAA -> Gate-All-Around. The gate surrounds the channel more completely, improving electrostatic control. Modern implementations commonly use stacked nanosheets.

Chiplet -> Instead of building an entire processor as one large die, designers can build multiple dies that work together as one system.

This can help with manufacturing, yield, scalability and mixing different technologies in the same product.

Advanced packaging -> Technologies used to connect dies, memory and other components with very high bandwidth and low power.

This includes things like 2.5D integration, 3D stacking, interposers and hybrid bonding.

HBM -> High Bandwidth Memory.

HBM stacks multiple DRAM dies and connects them through very wide memory interfaces, providing extremely high bandwidth.

This is one reason HBM has become so important for modern AI accelerators.

items.content:
One of the biggest mistakes beginners make when testing an application is not reading the error messages properly.

They send a payload, get an error and conclude that it did not work.

Then they send another payload, get another error and assume it is basically the same thing.

But an error does not mean the payload did not work. It just means that an error was triggered somewhere in the execution path, and that point may be after the interesting part already happened.

Your payload may have been parsed successfully, changed the control flow, bypassed a check, reached a different function or triggered behaviour that the previous payload did not. Something later may simply have failed.

This is why small differences matter so much. A different exception, a slightly different message, a different status code or even a different location in a stack trace can tell you that you moved forward.

Security testing is often about noticing those tiny changes and asking why they happened.

Don’t just look for success or failure.

Read the error.

items.content:
Detection engineers, red teamers and Active Directory people: NetNTLMv1 was supposed to be dying.

Outflank just gave it a new reason to stay on your threat model.

NTLMRain turns captured NetNTLMv1 responses into something much easier to work with:

WebGPU acceleration.
Browser-based cracking workflow.
Cross-platform CLI.
Native CPU fallback.
Public lookup service.
Reworked rainbow tables compressed to 3.99 TB.
Searchable in under a minute on fast storage.

The goal: recover NT hashes from NetNTLMv1 responses far more efficiently.

And the timing matters.

Microsoft has already removed the NTLMv1 protocol from Windows 11 24H2 / Server 2025, but NTLMv1-derived cryptography can still survive in scenarios such as MS-CHAPv2, with further enforcement coming.

Red teamers: old authentication weaknesses can still become credential-access primitives.

Detection engineers + blue teams: don't assume 'deprecated' means gone. Hunt the authentication paths, downgrade conditions and legacy dependencies that keep this alive.

Research by @c3c / @OutflankNL:
https://t.co/33lehDmKiE

NetNTLMv1 is dead.

Long live NetNTLMv1.

#DetectionEngineering #RedTeam #ActiveDirectory #Infosec

items.content:
RT @secparam: Apple's new "Reference Image" design suggests something Apple won't say out loud: they don't actually trust the iPhone's Secure Enclave that much. They're probably right, and that has implications both for other proposals to stop deepfakes and for privacy-preserving identity, if it ever gets beyond stopping kids from looking at porn.

Reference Image is a mode in the iPhone camera where Apple's servers sign a photo as genuine. The phone sends the raw data, signed by its trusted hardware, to Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers, which process it, apply edits, and sign the result. It hides who took the photo, though Apple appears to keep identifying data so it can revoke photos from hacked phones.

But why involve Apple's servers at all? It costs money and adds risk for Apple, like demands to deanonymize journalists, so they really have to get Private Compute Right.

Maybe Apple couldn't get the image pipeline running inside the Secure Enclave. I doubt it. They could have, or could have with some work.

But iPhones get jailbroken, and keys can be extracted from the Secure Enclave. If your threat model includes nation states making deepfakes, assume they'll do it. So I think Apple is using PCC as a trusted man-in-the-middle: it sees everything, so it can try to block exploited devices, and adapt as they see what attackers do.

The other thing that relies on secure hardware is privacy-preserving credentials. Google's zk-id proposal uses hardware device binding to prevent credential sharing, and you might want to verify biometrics at enrollment too. But if we start using this for privacy-preserving KYC in banking and cryptocurrency, or for proof of personhood and deepfake prevention on social media, attackers will try to steal credentials or buy and borrow legit accounts. Device binding is meant to stop this. Apple's design suggests they think it can't.

items.content:
RT @hackyboiz2: [1day-1line] CVE-2026-28666: Exposure of Untrusted RAW Decoders in SystemUI via a mimetype Check Bypass in Android LocalImageResolver

Hello, this is Libera.
Today's 1day-1line covers a check bypass in Android's notification image path.
Google added a mimetype allowlist to LocalImageResolver to keep the bug-prone RAW decoders out of the notification path, but the check was wired into only 1 of its 7 call sites.

As a result, an attacker app can run the blocked DNG decoder inside the SystemUI process with a single setLargeIcon() call. Depending on the decoded content, this can lead to a Persistent DoS or EOP.

Please refer to the blog post for more details (Root Cause, PoC, and Patch info)!
 https://t.co/hpHVIPzNob
